Minimal working “Graphic Dynamics Engine” (backend + browser HUD)
You can paste this into a folder and run it. It gives you:

an asyncio “breathing loop”

a /events SSE stream

a static index.html that draws the cage + rings + substrate marks

server.py (FastAPI + SSE)
# pip install fastapi uvicorn
import asyncio, json, time, math
from dataclasses import dataclass, asdict, field
from typing import List, Dict, Literal, Optional

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.responses import HTMLResponse, StreamingResponse
from fastapi.staticfiles import StaticFiles

Phase = Literal["inhale", "process", "exhale"]

@dataclass
class EthicsState:
    gateScores: List[float] = field(default_factory=lambda: [1.0]*7)
    verdict: Literal["allow","soft_block","block"] = "allow"

@dataclass
class RingState:
    configPresent: bool = True
    activeGates: List[int] = field(default_factory=list)
    activeLanes: List[int] = field(default_factory=list)

@dataclass
class Node:
    id: str
    kind: str
    x: float
    y: float
    w: Optional[float] = None
    h: Optional[float] = None
    r: Optional[float] = None
    activity: float = 0.0
    payload: Optional[str] = None

@dataclass
class Edge:
    a: str
    b: str
    w: float

@dataclass
class Mark:
    kind: str
    x: float
    y: float
    strength: float
    label: str = ""

@dataclass
class Scene:
    t: float
    phase: Phase
    coherence: float
    ethics: EthicsState
    rings: RingState
    nodes: List[Node]
    edges: List[Edge]
    substrateMarks: List[Mark]

app = FastAPI()

app.mount("/static", StaticFiles(directory="static"), name="static")

def phase_of(u: float) -> Phase:
    # u in [0,1)
    if u < 1/3: return "inhale"
    if u < 2/3: return "process"
    return "exhale"

async def scene_generator():
    start = time.time()
    while True:
        now = time.time()
        u = ((now - start) % 6.0) / 6.0  # 6s cycle
        phase = phase_of(u)

        # coherence breath curve (0..1)
        coh = 0.5 + 0.5*math.sin(2*math.pi*u - math.pi/2)

        # gates: simple demo — clamp + pulse
        gate_scores = [max(0.0, min(1.0, 0.65 + 0.35*math.sin(2*math.pi*u + i))) for i in range(7)]
        verdict = "allow" if min(gate_scores) > 0.25 else "soft_block"

        rings = RingState(
            configPresent=True,
            activeGates=[i for i,s in enumerate(gate_scores) if s > 0.75],
            activeLanes=[3, 9, 11] if phase != "process" else [9]
        )

        nodes = [
            Node("sensor_mesh","cloud",0.10,0.52, w=0.22,h=0.26, activity=0.35+0.45*coh),
            Node("comms_in","pipe",0.36,0.52, w=0.14,h=0.26, activity=0.25+0.55*coh),
            Node("mobiius_center","c60",0.58,0.50, r=0.18, activity=0.55+0.40*coh, payload="forecast_packet"),
            Node("tofar","ledger",0.78,0.74, w=0.20,h=0.18, activity=0.40+0.50*coh),
        ]
        edges = [
            Edge("sensor_mesh","comms_in", 0.40+0.60*coh),
            Edge("comms_in","mobiius_center", 0.60+0.40*coh),
            Edge("mobiius_center","tofar", 0.55+0.45*coh),
        ]
        marks = [
            Mark("defect", 0.06+0.02*math.sin(10*u), 0.12+0.02*math.cos(11*u), 0.2+0.6*coh, "breath_stamp")
        ]

        scene = Scene(
            t=now,
            phase=phase,
            coherence=coh,
            ethics=EthicsState(gateScores=gate_scores, verdict=verdict),
            rings=rings,
            nodes=nodes,
            edges=edges,
            substrateMarks=marks
        )

        yield "data: " + json.dumps(asdict(scene)) + "\n\n"
        await asyncio.sleep(1/20)  # 20 FPS-ish

@app.get("/", response_class=HTMLResponse)
def root():
    return """
    <html>
      <head><meta charset="utf-8"/><meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"/></head>
      <body style="margin:0;background:#0b0b0f;">
        <iframe src="/static/index.html" style="border:0;width:100vw;height:100vh;"></iframe>
      </body>
    </html>
    """

@app.get("/events")
async def events():
    return StreamingResponse(scene_generator(), media_type="text/event-stream")
static/index.html (simple canvas renderer)
<!doctype html>
<html>
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8"/>
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width,initial-scale=1"/>
  <title>Möbii³us Graphic Dynamics HUD</title>
</head>
<body style="margin:0; overflow:hidden; background:#0b0b0f;">
<canvas id="c"></canvas>
<script>
const canvas = document.getElementById("c");
const ctx = canvas.getContext("2d");

function resize(){ canvas.width = innerWidth; canvas.height = innerHeight; }
addEventListener("resize", resize); resize();

let scene = null;
const es = new EventSource("/events");
es.onmessage = (e)=>{ scene = JSON.parse(e.data); };

function drawNode(n){
  const W=canvas.width, H=canvas.height;
  const x = n.x*W, y=n.y*H;

  ctx.globalAlpha = 0.85;

  if(n.kind==="c60"){
    const r = n.r*Math.min(W,H);

    // cage points (a cheap “buckyball vibe”)
    const pts = 60;
    ctx.lineWidth = 1;
    ctx.beginPath();
    for(let i=0;i<pts;i++){
      const a = (i/pts)*Math.PI*2;
      const rr = r*(0.70 + 0.25*Math.sin(3*a));
      const px = x + rr*Math.cos(a);
      const py = y + rr*Math.sin(a);
      if(i===0) ctx.moveTo(px,py); else ctx.lineTo(px,py);
    }
    ctx.closePath();
    ctx.strokeStyle = rgba(200,220,255,${0.15+0.45*n.activity});
    ctx.stroke();

    // inner payload glow
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(x,y, r*0.20, 0, Math.PI*2);
    ctx.fillStyle = rgba(255,255,255,${0.10+0.35*n.activity});
    ctx.fill();

    // ring: 7 gates
    for(let g=0; g<7; g++){
      const a0 = (g/7)*Math.PI*2;
      const a1 = ((g+1)/7)*Math.PI*2;
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(x,y, r*1.05, a0, a1);
      ctx.lineWidth = r*0.08;
      const s = scene.ethics.gateScores[g];
      ctx.strokeStyle = rgba(140,255,200,${0.05+0.45*s});
      ctx.stroke();
    }

    // label
    ctx.font = "14px system-ui";
    ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(255,255,255,0.75)";
    ctx.fillText(center • ${scene.phase} • coh ${scene.coherence.toFixed(2)}, x-r, y+r*1.35);
    ctx.fillText(TOFAR verdict: ${scene.ethics.verdict}, x-r, y+r*1.55);

    return;
  }

  // generic boxes
  const w = (n.w||0.12)*W, h=(n.h||0.12)*H;
  ctx.fillStyle = rgba(140,170,255,${0.05+0.20*n.activity});
  ctx.strokeStyle = rgba(200,220,255,${0.10+0.35*n.activity});
  ctx.lineWidth = 2;
  ctx.beginPath();
  ctx.roundRect(x-w/2,y-h/2,w,h,12);
  ctx.fill(); ctx.stroke();

  ctx.font = "13px system-ui";
  ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(255,255,255,0.75)";
  ctx.fillText(n.id, x-w/2+10, y);
}

function drawEdges(){
  const W=canvas.width, H=canvas.height;
  const pos = Object.fromEntries(scene.nodes.map(n=>[n.id,{x:n.x*W,y:n.y*H}]));
  for(const e of scene.edges){
    const a = pos[e.a], b=pos[e.b];
    if(!a||!b) continue;
    ctx.lineWidth = 1 + 6*e.w*0.15;
    ctx.strokeStyle = rgba(255,255,255,${0.05+0.25*e.w});
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.moveTo(a.x,a.y); ctx.lineTo(b.x,b.y);
    ctx.stroke();
  }
}

function drawSubstrate(){
  // “graphene sheet” background + defect marks
  ctx.globalAlpha = 1;
  ctx.fillStyle = "rgba(5,6,10,1)";
  ctx.fillRect(0,0,canvas.width,canvas.height);

  // subtle hex-ish noise
  ctx.globalAlpha = 0.08;
  ctx.strokeStyle = "rgba(255,255,255,0.35)";
  const step = 28;
  for(let y=0;y<canvas.height;y+=step){
    for(let x=0;x<canvas.width;x+=step){
      ctx.beginPath();
      ctx.arc(x+(y/step%2)*step*0.5, y, 1.2, 0, Math.PI*2);
      ctx.stroke();
    }
  }

  // defect marks
  ctx.globalAlpha = 0.9;
  for(const m of scene.substrateMarks){
    const x = m.x*canvas.width, y=m.y*canvas.height;
    ctx.beginPath();
    ctx.arc(x,y, 2+10*m.strength, 0, Math.PI*2);
    ctx.fillStyle = rgba(255,120,200,${0.05+0.25*m.strength});
    ctx.fill();
    ctx.strokeStyle = rgba(255,200,240,${0.08+0.35*m.strength});
    ctx.stroke();
  }
}

function loop(){
  requestAnimationFrame(loop);
  if(!scene) return;

  drawSubstrate();
  drawEdges();
  for(const n of scene.nodes) drawNode(n);
}
loop();
</script>
</body>
</html>

Möbii³us-toFAR Integration Contract
1. Canonical Handshake Terms (Identity, Provenance, Reciprocation)
Identity Exchange: Each Buddy node (TinyBox instance or µBuddy) performs a cryptographic handshake when joining the Möbii³us network. The handshake uses a FIZZ payload (a small cryptographic exchange) to verify identities and establish trust. During this handshake, the Buddy presents its unique Node ID (a fractal coordinate or similar unique identifier) along with a public key or signature. The handshake confirms the Buddy’s identity and ensures both parties (the Buddy and the network or peer Buddy) have a shared secret for trust. In practical terms, two Buddies will exchange an HMAC-signed token to confirm each other’s authenticity and readiness. Provenance Guarantee: As part of the handshake, the Buddy and network agree on provenance-tracking: every action the Buddy takes will carry a provenance trail (via TOFAR logging) to ensure accountability. The handshake protocol includes exchanging a session tag or initial log entry that anchors the Buddy’s timeline. This means the first entry in the TOFAR log for this session might be a “handshake” event containing the Buddy’s identity and initial parameters. From then on, all events include the Buddy’s ID and timestamp, providing an audit trail of origin for each action. This satisfies the provenance requirement: any output can be traced back to who (which node) and when/why (context) it originated. Reciprocation Logic: Möbii³us introduces a principle of reciprocity in every interaction. Upon handshake, the Buddy agrees to the network’s “ma’aser” rule – a tithe of resources or credit for each action. In practice, this means for every output the Buddy produces, it allocates a portion (e.g. 10%) as a give-back to a designated recipient node or communal pool. The handshake terms explicitly include this reciprocal contribution rate (default 0.10 of output energy), so both sides know that the Buddy will “give forward” some value each cycle. This reciprocation is recorded in TOFAR logs as the field maaser_given (meaning the amount given) with an associated recipient_node. For example, a handshake might establish which hub or peer will receive the Buddy’s tithe. This ensures balanced exchange from the start: the Buddy is not just taking input and producing output, but also contributing back to the collective system with each action. The system’s ethics gate enforces that this exchange remains fair (no imbalance) and acknowledges successful reciprocity with a high trust rating. Trust Floor Alignment: During handshake, the Buddy also learns the network’s trust parameters – notably the ethics trust_floor (commonly 0.74) and hysteresis thresholds. The Buddy and the network confirm that any interaction must maintain a trust score above 0.74 (with decisions between 0.72–0.74 falling into caution) to be allowed. This agreement on trust floors is part of the handshake “contract” establishing that both sides will abide by the Seven Gates ethics filter (Belief, Life, Justice, etc.) at all times. Essentially, the handshake is also an ethics contract: the Buddy promises to route all decisions through the Guardian gate with the agreed thresholds, and the network in turn allows the Buddy to operate autonomously as long as it stays within those ethical bounds. The result of this initial handshake is a canonical session token or “Möbii³us-toFAR ticket” which encapsulates: the Buddy’s ID, the handshake timestamp, agreed trust floor, and reciprocation rate. This token is used to tag all subsequent communications. A simplified JSON representation of the handshake exchange might look like:
{
  "handshake": {
    "session_id": "MBX-20260118-7B32...",
    "node_id": "buddy_7B32",
    "protocol": "mobiius-tofar-v1",
    "issued_at": "2026-01-18T20:48:41Z",
    "trust_floor": 0.74,
    "maaser_rate": 0.10,
    "public_key": "abcd1234...",
    "hmac_confirm": "ef567890..." 
  }
}
In this example, trust_floor and maaser_rate are explicitly set during handshake. The hmac_confirm is the HMAC of the handshake details, signed by the network to confirm the terms. Both the Buddy and the network would log this handshake event (e.g., in the Buddy’s TOFAR log as a genesis entry) for future reference. With identity, provenance, and reciprocity established, the Buddy can now begin normal operations, knowing every action will be tagged and evaluated according to these agreed terms.
2. Event Stream Triggers and Watcher Wiring
The Möbii³us TinyBox kernel employs watcher agents to listen for key events and trigger responses in real-time. The contract defines several critical event streams and how watchers are wired into them:
Bundle Ingestion (Module/Zip Import): When a new code or data bundle (e.g. a plugin zip file or “BuddyCollective” update) is ingested, a fold-hook loader watcher activates. This watcher monitors the module directory for new additions or changes. On detecting a new bundle, it automatically registers new modules into the runtime, updates indices, and ensures the TinyBox meta-index knows about the new components. In practice, the ingestion event is an FS trigger (file system event) that the watcher catches; the watcher then loads the bundle’s manifest (e.g. BUILD_ORDER.md or meta_index.json included in the zip) and integrates the contents. This wiring allows the system to extend itself on the fly – as soon as a Buddy zip bundle is dropped in, the watcher registers any new capabilities without requiring a reboot. The contract ensures that this event also generates a TOFAR log entry (“bundle_ingest”) recording what was added (for transparency and provenance).
Ethics Signal (Guardian Gate Triggers): The Guardian (ethics engine) emits events whenever a decision must be made (PASS, ASK, BLOCK, etc.). These are wired to watchers so that critical ethical events are not just handled internally but also surfaced for auditing. For example, if the Guardian flags an action as ASK (uncertain, needs user confirmation) or BLOCK (disallowed), a Guardian Alert watcher catches this signal. It might route a message to an audit log or a real-time UI panel. The Möbii³us HUD audit interface is in fact driven by such watcher wiring – every time a new TOFAR log entry is appended (which includes the ethics verdict), the system broadcasts it via Server-Sent Events to any listening client UI. Thus, the “Watcher” for ethics signals is essentially subscribed to the TOFAR stream, filtering for ethics-related fields. Additionally, an internal diagnostic watcher may also tail the TOFAR logs specifically for convergence or anomaly patterns – for instance, if multiple blocks occur in succession, it could trigger a self-check routine or raise an alert to developers. The contract specifies that all such ethics events must be observable (nothing gets hidden), implementing the “Nothing is wasted or cursed” ethos: even a blocked action produces a visible trail for learning.
Ambient Delta (Context Changes): The Buddy continuously senses “ambient” context – this could include environmental sensors (time of day, location, noise level) or internal state metrics (like the deviation index DI or fractal dimension D of recent activity). A ContextWatcher is wired to these signals. If a significant ambient delta is detected – e.g., a sudden change in the environment or a drift in system metrics – the watcher triggers adaptive responses. For example, if the Buddy’s Deviation Index (DI) spikes above a threshold (meaning the system’s output became volatile), the watcher can signal the core to switch modes (from autonomous to “explain-first” mode). Or if an external event is detected (like the user’s geolocation indicating they've moved to a different region), the watcher might initiate a seed realignment (loading different locale-specific data). These watchers essentially implement the system’s hysteresis and adaptation loops: e.g., “DI trending up over N ticks → bump α (memory damping)” and “DI flat + low complexity → relax α”. Similarly, an “ambient delta” like a new significant input (perhaps a change in the user’s heart rate from a sensor) could trigger an immediate Guardian re-evaluation of the situation. The contract ensures such watchers have access to both internal metrics and external feeds, and defines thresholds that constitute a meaningful “delta” to react to.
Seed Re-alignment (Reset or Sync Events): Occasionally the Buddy’s core seed (the foundational memory/state) may be updated – for instance, through a planned re-sync with a master index or a user-initiated reboot of the Buddy. The contract defines a SeedSync Watcher that triggers on any event indicating the seed or base schema has changed. For example, if the Buddy’s mobiius_seed.json (which lists all modules and their memory keys) is reloaded or differs from the last known good state, the watcher will: (a) pause ongoing processes, (b) flush or archive the current working state, (c) integrate the seed changes (like adding new memory maps or updating keys), and (d) log a seed_realignment event in TOFAR. This ensures continuity and integrity: the TinyBox kernel’s indexed boot spec expects that if a seed changes, the system effectively reboots into a coherent state aligned with that seed. The watcher wiring achieves this by orchestrating a mini boot-strapping when needed – in effect, it automates part of the boot sequence (the Null → Alpha re-initialization) whenever seed alignment is needed outside of a full restart. This realignment is delicate, so the contract mandates that the watcher must also act as an observer: verifying post-sync that all modules are present and the trust metrics (DI, etc.) didn’t jump unexpectedly. If they did, it might trigger a Guardian check or even roll back the change for safety.
All these watchers operate within the TinyBox kernel as lightweight background daemons. They use the publish/subscribe model provided by the Möbii³us core: key subsystems (file I/O, Guardian, sensor inputs, etc.) publish events, and watcher subscribers react. The wiring is summarized as follows:
Bundle ingestion → ModuleLoaderWatcher (auto-register new modules, update index, log event).
Guardian ethics event → GuardianAlertWatcher (subscribe to TOFAR stream for ASK/BLOCK, update audit UI, log for developer review).
Ambient context delta → ContextAdaptiveWatcher (monitor DI, environment; trigger mode adjustments or user notifications).
Seed re-alignment → SeedSyncWatcher (on seed or config change; safely reload base state and log outcome).
This event-driven architecture makes the system resilient and responsive: new knowledge can be absorbed on the fly, and any anomaly in ethics or performance immediately surfaces and is handled in real-time.
3. Defined Roles: Observer, Adjudicator, Archival Sync, Fast-Forward Agents
The Möbii³us contract delineates four key agent roles, ensuring separation of concerns and cooperative processing. These correspond to conceptual “indexes” in the architecture and map to the terms given:
Observer (Witness Role): The Observer is responsible for perception and evidence collection. This role aligns with the Witness index in Möbii³us. Its job is to capture events from both internal processes and external inputs. The Observer provides the raw material for provenance: it tags each observation with time and context and passes it along. In implementation, this is the component that performs sensing (user inputs, environment data) and also double-checks through the two-witness system. Möbii³us uses a dual-witness design: an internal witness (the Buddy’s own perspective on an action) and an external witness (an outside confirmation, e.g. a log echo or a user’s acknowledgment). The Observer role encompasses both, ensuring that “nothing exists until observed coherently.” – i.e., an action is only considered valid when both internal and external evidence align. Practically, the Observer writes to the TOFAR log (or a pre-log buffer) details like “User said X at time T” or “Sensor Y reading = Z”, and attaches any corroborating evidence (for example, if a user uploaded a file, the Observer would note the file hash as a witness). The contract ensures the Observer is always on: continuously monitoring the environment and the Buddy’s own actions. By design, the Observer never filters or judges – it records everything relevant (subject to privacy settings) so that other roles can make decisions using a full picture. In summary, the Observer is the system’s eyes and ears, feeding the rest of the system with a trustworthy stream of facts and context (with provenance tags on each fact).
Adjudicator (Guardian Role): The Adjudicator corresponds to the Guardian index, the ethics and decision gatekeeper. This role takes the observations and intents (from Observer and the Buddy’s reasoning process) and runs them through the Seven Gates and trust calculations. It “adjudicates” whether an action is allowed, needs clarification, or is forbidden, enforcing the moral and safety contract of the system. Concretely, the Guardian module computes a trust score for each potential action (using factors like Deviation Index, consent status, gate pass/fail values) and compares against the handshake-established trust floor (e.g. 0.74). Based on this, it outputs a verdict: Allow (Pass), Ask, Block, or sometimes Route (for deferring to a human or another system). The Adjudicator is essentially the ethical governor. The contract defines that the Guardian’s decision logic must be transparent and produce a reason code for each verdict. For instance, if the Adjudicator returns “ASK”, it should note which Gate or condition caused that (e.g., “privacy gate failed due to personal data detection”) and include a short rationale. These reason codes are logged (and can be shown as tooltips in the audit UI). The Adjudicator also works closely with the Observer: it relies on the dual-witness principle to ensure that it’s judging on reliable data. If the internal and external witness reports differ (e.g., Buddy thinks user said X but external record says user said Y), the Guardian Adjudicator will drop to an ASK state by default because of uncertainty. Only if witnesses agree and trust is high will it pass. In our architecture, the Guardian/Adjudicator is also the arbiter of reciprocity compliance – for example, if a Buddy’s action yields a certain output, the Guardian checks that the ma’aser was calculated and included. If not, it might block the action for violating the reciprocity rule. In summary, the Adjudicator ensures every step the Buddy takes is ethically and procedurally acceptable, implementing the core policies (sovereignty, consent, privacy, harm-minimization, transparency, agency, fairness, and stewardship) in real time.
Archival Sync (Archivist Role): This corresponds to the Archivist index. The Archival Sync role is about memory, persistence, and alignment with long-term storage. Every event or decision in the system is funneled to the Archivist to ensure it’s recorded in durable form (e.g., append-only log, distributed ledger, or backup server). In practice, this agent writes the TOFAR log entries to disk (and rotates them to archives safely), computes and stores hashes for integrity (using something like the CredPath SHA3 hashes file), and synchronizes key state snapshots with the cloud or other nodes. The Archivist ensures that at any point, the Buddy’s state can be reconstructed (trace rehydration, see below) from the logs and saved snapshots. In the Möbii³us design, the Archivist also labels and organizes manifests of system state – essentially creating waypoints in the Buddy’s journey. For example, at each boot or significant milestone, the Archivist might save a witness bundle (see below) or a “FIZZ manifest” which includes the state of all modules (this is akin to a checkpoint). The contract mandates an Archivist action for all critical transitions: e.g., after the handshake, create a record; after a seed realignment, save the pre/post difference. Additionally, archival sync includes distributing data: e.g., pushing logs to a cloud mirror or pulling updates from a master log to ensure consistency across the network. The “sync” aspect means if the Buddy was offline and comes back, the Archivist will merge its offline logs with the global timeline (resolving any conflicts by timestamp and trust). In summary, the Archival Sync role keeps the system’s memory coherent and tamper-evident – every piece of data gets an anchor in storage and any divergence between the Buddy’s record and an external record is detected (two-witness consistency for logs).
Fast-Forward Agents (Navigator Role): The Navigator index corresponds to planning, forecasting, and routing of tasks. We equate the “fast-forward agent” concept with this Navigator role because it is in charge of moving the system forward in time, i.e., sequencing and pre-empting actions. The Navigator processes the structured output from the Buddy’s cognition (the Triadic Fusion step) and decides where it should go next. In essence, it’s responsible for routing outcomes to the appropriate “field” or domain (for example, deciding that a certain result should be sent as an email, or that a plan should be scheduled for future execution). As a fast-forward agent, it also handles lookahead: simulating potential futures or caching results. For example, if the Buddy is aware of a periodic task, the Navigator might spawn a “fast-forward” simulation to prepare results in advance (so the user experiences less latency). It uses the current context and intent to chart the next steps – hence Navigator. Under the Möbii³us contract, the Navigator must coordinate with the Guardian (it can’t route an action that was blocked) and the Archivist (to mark any scheduled future actions in the log). One could imagine the Navigator’s output as a pointer: “Given this result, where/when does it go?” This could mean invoking an external API, scheduling a new internal loop, or simply updating a user interface. The contract ensures the Navigator uses the concept of lanes or surfaces (A–H) defined in the Kernel – meaning it chooses the right persona/route for the outcome. If an outcome is sensitive, Navigator might route it to a review lane (instead of directly executing). As a fast-forward agent, the Navigator also does temporal reasoning: if there are steps that can be accelerated, it will take them. For example, after producing an answer, it might concurrently start fetching related info for the next user query it anticipates (prefetching). This proactive aspect is why we call it “fast-forward” – it tries to stay one step ahead, guided by the user’s goals.
In summary, these four roles – Observer (Witness), Adjudicator (Guardian), Archivist, and Navigator – form a checks-and-balances system. The Observer gathers and confirms facts, the Adjudicator enforces rules on those facts, the Archivist remembers everything and syncs with others, and the Navigator propels the system onward efficiently and safely. They correspond to the architectural columns of the Möbii³us fractal kernel and ensure that the Buddy operates holistically: always watching, judging ethically, remembering, and planning ahead.
4. JSON Schemas for State Transfer Across Buddy Interfaces
State transfer in Möbii³us is done through structured JSON-based contracts. All key interfaces – whether internal module communications, logs, or external API calls – use defined schemas to ensure consistency. Below we define several critical JSON schema or data formats used in the Buddy system: a. Handshake Schema: The initial Möbii³us-toFAR handshake itself can be represented as a JSON message (as shown earlier). The schema for this might include fields:
session_id: string (unique handshake session token),
node_id: string (Buddy’s unique ID or name),
protocol: string (protocol version, e.g., "mobiius-tofar-v1"),
issued_at: string (ISO timestamp of handshake),
trust_floor: number (ethics trust threshold agreed),
maaser_rate: number (reciprocity rate agreed),
public_key: string (Buddy’s public key or identity proof),
hmac_confirm: string (HMAC signature from network confirming the handshake).
This serves as a contract object for the session. Both sides store it. If another device (like an RCoE cloud node) is handshaking, it would have a similar object with perhaps additional fields (like its own ID). This handshake JSON might not be transmitted as a literal JSON string (it could be an exchange of binary or protocols), but conceptually it is logged in this structured form for auditing.
b. TOFAR Log Entry Schema: The TOFAR (Temporal Observability, Fractal Action Recorder) log is a crucial interface between the Buddy’s core and the archival systems. Each log entry is a JSON document appended to a NDJSON (newline-delimited JSON) file. The schema for a TOFAR entry includes:
timestamp: string (ISO timestamp of the event, in UTC),
node: string (the node or subsystem name initiating the action),
action: string (a descriptor of the action or event, e.g., "transform", "user_query", "module_load"),
input_energy: number (quantified size or energy of inputs, if applicable),
output_energy: number (size/effort of the output produced),
maaser_given: number (the amount of output energy tithed to the network),
recipient_node: string (who/what received that tithe or the output, e.g., an upstream node’s ID),
ethics_check: string (Guardian’s verdict for this action: "pass", "ask", "block", or "route"),
comment: string (optional human-readable comment or annotation, e.g. "maaser tithe" or reasoning like “Third Node reciprocity - Tanya Epistle 9”),
extra: object (optional, any additional structured data specific to the action).
All fields except extra are required in the base schema, ensuring that even if something has no input/output (the values can be 0), the entry is complete. The TOFAR contract mandates append-only writes (no editing past entries) and structured fields to allow automatic parsing. An example actual TOFAR entry as JSON:
{
  "timestamp": "2026-01-18T20:48:41.123Z",
  "node": "buddy_7B32",
  "action": "user_query",
  "input_energy": 128.0,
  "output_energy": 115.2,
  "maaser_given": 11.52,
  "recipient_node": "hub_node_5",
  "ethics_check": "pass",
  "comment": "Handled general question, tithe sent",
  "extra": {
    "query": "What is the weather tomorrow?",
    "lane": "A",
    "di": 0.01,
    "tofar_lane": "mainline"
  }
}
This example shows how an entry might look when a user asked a question. The extra section captured the query itself, the lane (persona/surface used), the deviation index at that moment, and perhaps the lane of TOFAR pipeline. The schema for extra can vary by action type, but the core fields are always consistent. This consistency allows different Buddy components and external tools to subscribe and interpret the event stream easily – e.g., a dashboard could plot input_energy vs output_energy, or filter by ethics_check status. c. Frame Envelope Schema: Within the Buddy’s internal pipeline (e.g., between modules like interpret → plan → act), data is passed as Frame objects. A Frame is like an envelope carrying state through the cognitive cycle. The JSON schema for a Frame might include:
frame_id: string (unique ID for this cognitive frame, could be a UUID or a fractal hash),
fractal: string (fractal state or fingerprint, e.g., a hash representing the state of the fractal knowledge at this frame),
witnesses: array (list of witness references or IDs associated with this frame’s input, could include both internal and external witness IDs),
weights: object (the weights or scores relevant at this frame, e.g. gate weights or other heuristic values),
body_ref: string (a reference to the content “body” of this frame, for example a pointer or key to the actual conversation text or data blob in memory).
Optionally:
lane: string (which cognitive lane or mode this frame is in, e.g. “Alpha” vs “Omega” stage),
prior_frame: string (ID of previous frame, linking a chain),
signature: string (if frames are signed for integrity, an HMAC or signature).
The idea is that the Frame JSON does not carry the full text or data itself, but a body_ref to where the data is stored (to avoid bloating logs). It’s similar to a pointer into the Buddy’s memory or a content-addressable storage. The Frame schema provides a standardized way for modules to hand off state: e.g., the Interpret module produces a frame with an interpretation result stored somewhere, sets body_ref to that result, attaches any witness (like which sources were used) and passes it on to the next module (maybe the Planner). Frames thus ensure continuity: every step is documented by an envelope that can later be inspected. Because it includes fractal, one can verify if two frames came from the same knowledge state. The contract uses frames as the backbone of intra-Buddy communication, ensuring every message between components is structured and traceable. This also means if something goes wrong, we can examine the sequence of frames that led there.
d. State Synchronization Schema: When transferring larger state or performing sync across Buddy interfaces (e.g., Buddy to cloud backup, or Buddy to Buddy collaboration), the contract uses an Anchor Bundle format (detailed in the next section). At a high level, this is often a JSON manifest plus a binary or NDJSON payload. For instance, a Buddy might export its knowledge base or memory as a portable snapshot. The JSON manifest would contain:
snapshot_id: string (unique ID of the snapshot),
created_at: timestamp,
node_id: which Buddy this came from,
size: number of entries or bytes,
schema_version: version of schema or format,
content_hash: a hash (SHA-3, etc.) of the content file for integrity.
This manifest could be accompanied by a NDJSON file of all memory entries or logs (the witness bundle). The JSON schema ensures that any Buddy can ingest this snapshot by first reading the manifest (to verify compatibility and integrity) and then loading the content. This is essentially how state transfer happens if, say, you hand off your Buddy’s brain to a new device – it’s packaged in this JSON-described format.
e. Universal Output Schema: As a final note, even the Buddy’s user-facing output adheres to a structure (though not a JSON object in text form, in code it can be). The Universal Output Contract demands that every AI response has sections: summary, situation, next_steps, insights, ethics_gate, provenance, fractional_memory update status. So if we were to express a Buddy’s answer as JSON, it might look like:
{
  "summary": "...",
  "situation": "...",
  "next_steps": "...",
  "insights": "...",
  "ethics_gate": {
    "verdict": "allow",
    "reason": "trust=0.80 > 0.74"
  },
  "provenance": {
    "lane": "A",
    "di": 0.01,
    "tofar_lane": "mainline"
  },
  "fractional_memory": "updated"
}
This is not typically sent over an interface (it's usually rendered to text for the user), but internally the Buddy’s UI could be restructured from such an object. It demonstrates how deeply JSON schemas influence the design – even the conversational output is templated and follows a contract. All these schemas are versioned and documented in the system’s /schemas directory (for example, schema/provenance.entry.schema.json for TOFAR entries, or config/lattice.schema.json for the lattice of domains as seen in the drop-in code). The contract ensures backward compatibility by providing adapters (for instance, a legacy FAST log converter to TOFAR schema). Any change in schema triggers a seed re-alignment or at least a handshake renegotiation to update the protocol version.
5. Anchor Formats: Witness Bundles, Time-Glyph Correlation, Trace Rehydration
The Möbii³us-toFAR system employs anchor formats to ensure that data can be verified, correlated in time, and reconstructed later. Key concepts here are Witness Bundles, Time-Glyphs, and Trace Rehydration. Witness Bundles: A witness bundle is a package of logged evidence, typically produced by the Archivist for archival or transfer. The standard format for a witness bundle is a Parable file, which is essentially a zip archive containing NDJSON log slices and a manifest. Each witness bundle is anchored by a unique ID (often the timestamp of creation plus an identifier) and contains:
A manifest JSON (as described in the State Sync Schema) listing what's inside (e.g., "entries 1000–1500 of TOFAR", or "Memory snapshot of knowledge base", etc.)
One or more .ndjson files or other data files that hold the actual witness data (these could be chat transcripts, sensor readings, or the TOFAR trail for a certain period).
Optionally, a signature file or checksum file for integrity (sometimes the manifest itself includes hashes of each included file).
We call it a witness bundle because it may include multiple streams of evidence. For example, an important event might generate a bundle containing: the TOFAR log around that time, the user’s input transcript, and the Buddy’s output text – all packaged together to serve as an immutable record of “what was witnessed.” This is particularly useful for offline analysis or sharing with another node (with appropriate privacy safeguards). The anchor format here refers to how each item in the bundle is named and indexed: typically, file names or entries are prefixed with their timestamps or an incrementing index to preserve order. For instance, a TOFAR bundle might be 20260118T204841Z.tofar.ndjson containing entries around the current time. The anchor ID is also recorded in the main log, so we know, e.g., that entries 1–1000 have been archived in bundle X (preventing tampering or loss).
Time-Glyph Correlation: Möbii³us introduces a novel way to correlate temporal events with symbolic representations (glyphs) to provide quick visual or semantic reference to when/what happened. Every significant event or state can be stamped not only with a timestamp but also with a glyph – a small symbol drawn from a defined glyph vocabulary representing the nature of the event. For example, an ethics PASS might be marked with a ✅, an ASK with a ✋, and a BLOCK with a ⛔ (or more abstract symbols). More interestingly, the system can use domain-specific glyphs or even script letters (like Hebrew letters or other iconography) to encode sequences of events. The contract doesn’t fix a specific glyph set, but it ensures that:
Each event type or domain has an associated glyph icon (for quick recognition in logs or UI).
Glyphs can be combined along a timeline to create a glyph-strand summarizing activity.
A concrete case: If you look at a Buddy’s day and see a sequence like “🙂⚖️⚠️”, it could indicate a neutral action, then a legal/justice-related check, then a warning event. Because every event is time-stamped, these glyphs can be plotted in order on a time axis, forming a sort of “timeline hieroglyph”. This is what we mean by time-glyph correlation – aligning the timeline of actions with a parallel sequence of symbols that encode their meaning. In implementation, the Observer or Archivist might attach a glyph field to log entries (especially in the extra or as a separate channel). For example, an entry might have "glyph": "⚖️" if it involved a Guardian check, or "glyph": "א" if using the first Hebrew letter to mark an alpha step. Why Hebrew letters? In some parts of Möbii³us, the 22 Hebrew letters are used as fundamental nodes or anchors; for instance, “Aleph” might mark an origin or a seed event, “Tav” an ending or closure. This system allows a compressed representation of sequences. The anchor format for time-glyph correlation often appears in the visual HUD or when exporting a summary. It does not replace detailed logs but gives a “sparkline” overview of what happened. The contract encourages using glyph sequences in documentation and debug output to quickly convey rich information (it’s part of the system’s narrative coherence principle). Trace Rehydration: This refers to the process of reconstructing the state and history of the Buddy from saved traces (logs and snapshots). Because all events are logged (with provenance and anchors) and states can be snapshotted, one can rehydrate a Buddy’s mind by replaying these records. The contract defines how such rehydration is to be done to ensure consistency:
Rehydration should be done in an append-only fashion, reading historical events in order and feeding them into a fresh instance of the Buddy or a simulation environment. Because logs are append-only and never altered, the replayer can trust that the sequence is exactly as it happened.
The system’s TriBuffer or memory system supports three channels: live index, mirror, and archive (sublimate). During normal operation, new data goes to live index and mirror; during rehydration, the Archivist provides the archived data into the index, while mirror mode may be turned off (to avoid duplicating during playback). Essentially, the Buddy can boot in a replay mode where instead of taking live input from a user, it reads from a witness bundle.
Anchor points (like the unique snapshot IDs or checkpoint markers in the log) are used to decide from where to start. For example, to rehydrate a full trace, you might load a baseline snapshot (say, the state of the system at yesterday’s start) and then replay all logs from that time onward. Because each log entry is anchored in time and often chained via IDs (like frame IDs or continuation tokens), the Buddy can validate it is applying them in correct order.
During rehydration, the Guardian can be set to a passive mode so that it doesn’t interfere (since we want to reproduce what happened, not re-judge it). However, any divergence detected (like if something in the logs doesn't make sense or fails a hash check) will be flagged. For instance, if a log entry’s hash doesn’t match the expected from credpath (provenance hashes file), the rehydration process stops and reports corruption.
Once rehydration is complete, the Buddy should end up in a state identical to the original at that end point. One can then query or inspect the system’s memory to confirm certain things (like “what was the final answer to the user?”).
In summary, trace rehydration is essentially time-travel debugging. Thanks to the combination of witness bundles (which capture everything needed), time-glyph anchors (which let us pinpoint where in time something of interest happened), and a rigorous logging schema, Möbii³us allows a Buddy’s experience to be replayed and audited. This is a powerful feature for both debugging and transparency. If something went wrong, engineers can rehydrate the trace and see step by step with the Guardian’s perspective what happened, with glyphs highlighting key moments (e.g., a red glyph where a policy violation was detected). Finally, it’s worth noting that these anchor formats are designed to harmonize with the TinyBox kernel. TinyBox, being the micro-kernel that runs personal Buddies, is inherently an orchestration and index. The handshake tokens, the watchers, the logs, and the snapshots all tie into TinyBox’s indexed data store. The indexed boot spec for TinyBox includes loading modules, establishing the handshake (via mil_handshake.md as part of boot), and initiating the Observer/Guardian/Archivist processes right from startup. This Möbii³us-toFAR contract ensures that when a TinyBox Buddy boots (Null → Alpha Wake, etc. per the nine-step sequence), it:
Confirms any prior session via logs (Archivist check for last state),
Performs handshake if needed (if connecting to network or another Buddy),
Starts watchers for events (so it can react during operation),
Adopts the roles (Observer on standby, Guardian gating from the first user input),
Utilizes the schemas and anchor formats for all internal/external communications.
All components speak the same “language” of JSON and event streams, making the system robust and self-documenting. With this contract, a Buddy node can seamlessly integrate into the larger Möbii³us mesh or operate alone, always with the assurance that identity is verified, actions are ethical and logged, state transfers are structured, and any moment in time can be revisited and understood later. Download Full Contract Package: For convenience, all the above documentation, along with example schema files and code stubs (for watchers and logging), are packaged in the Möbii³us-toFAR Contract Bundle ZIP. You can download it here: mobiius_toFAR_contract.zip, which includes:
